title: Networking Foundations
summary: Understand networking as giving first and building genuine relationships, use weak ties, set a clear goal and find people through college, alumni and online communities.
objectives: Explain networking as building relationships rather than collecting favours.
Describe why weak ties often open doors and how to use them.
Set a networking goal and list five places to find the right people.

explanation.heading: What networking really is
explanation.body:
Many students hear "networking" and picture awkward events where people hand out cards and ask for jobs. That picture is wrong, and it makes people avoid something useful. **Networking** is simply building and maintaining genuine professional relationships: people who know what you do, whom you trust, and who might share information, advice or an introduction. In India a large share of jobs and opportunities travel through conversations, and for an entry-level candidate with no experience, a few good relationships can matter as much as a perfect CV.

The core principle is **giving first**. Instead of asking "What can I get?", ask "How can I be useful?" Useful can be small: sharing an article, congratulating someone on a project, answering a question in a community, or offering your notes. Giving builds goodwill and makes later requests natural.

explanation.heading: Weak ties and your starting network
explanation.body:
Sociologist Mark Granovetter found in his research that people often learn about jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. These acquaintances are **weak ties**. Your close friends know the same people and information you do. A weak tie, such as a senior from college now working at a services firm, moves in a different circle and sees opportunities you cannot.

So you do not need dozens of close friends in the industry. You need a wide set of light, friendly connections and the habit of keeping them warm. Everyone starts with more than they think: classmates, teachers, seniors, internship supervisors, relatives' colleagues and people you meet on courses.

explanation.heading: Start with a goal
explanation.body:
Networking without direction becomes random. Write a one-line **goal**: "In the next three months I want to understand what an entry-level ABAP consultant does day to day, and meet four people who work in SAP." This tells you who to look for and what to ask. Goals can also be to learn about a company, get feedback on your CV, or find a study partner.

A useful split is learn, connect, contribute. Learn means gaining information; connect means meeting people; contribute means giving something back. A healthy week has a bit of each.

explanation.heading: Where to find people
explanation.body:
Look first where trust already exists. **College**: teachers, placement cell, seniors and alumni, many of whom enjoy helping juniors from their own institution. **Communities**: SAP learning groups, local developer meetups, college clubs and student chapters of professional bodies. **Online**: LinkedIn, professional forums and open-source or learning communities where you can answer questions and share small projects. **Events**: webinars, workshops and college seminars.

Example: Aman wants to learn about SAP careers. He lists five places: his placement cell, two alumni from his BCA batch, an SAP forum, a local meetup and a teacher who once worked in a consulting firm. In a week he has identified three specific people to contact. Quality beats quantity: five real conversations beat 500 unanswered connection requests.

examples.title: Giving first in practice
examples.body: Meena sees a senior post on LinkedIn that his team is looking for interns. She does not message him asking for a referral. She comments with a useful link to a free SQL practice set, thanks him for sharing, and weeks later asks him two questions about his day-to-day work. He replies warmly and mentions a vacancy.
examples.takeaway: Small, genuine contributions create goodwill, and the opportunity followed from the relationship rather than a demand.

examples.title: A weak tie in action
examples.body: Imran's close friends all apply to the same three companies. A former classmate, whom he talks to only occasionally, mentions that a mid-sized consulting firm is hiring freshers for an ABAP training batch. Imran applies and gets interviewed.
examples.takeaway: Distant acquaintances reach different circles, so they surface opportunities your close circle never sees.

exercises.prompt: Which approach best reflects giving first?
options: Sharing a helpful resource and thanking someone for their post
Messaging a stranger for a job on day one
Collecting as many contacts as possible
Waiting for others to approach you
exercises.why: Giving builds goodwill without demanding anything. Asking for a job immediately or collecting contacts does not create a relationship.

exercises.prompt: People you know slightly, such as an old classmate in another company, are called weak ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Weak ties connect you to different circles and often bring new information.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best networking goal?
options: Speak to four people working in SAP in three months to learn about the role
exercises.why: It is specific, measurable and tied to learning. The others are vague or purely outcome-based.

exercises.prompt: List five specific places or groups, relevant to you, where you could meet people in your target field. For each, write one low-pressure thing you could do or give there this month.
exercises.modelAnswer: One: placement cell, ask for a list of alumni in IT services. Two: my BCA alumni group, congratulate a senior on a new role. Three: a local developer meetup, attend one session and ask one question. Four: an SAP forum, answer one beginner question. Five: my teacher with consulting experience, ask for advice on the first year of work and offer to share my project.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer lists real places you can reach, mixes college, community and online, and gives each a small action that is more about learning or giving than asking for a job. Avoid vague entries like "LinkedIn" with no action. Score yourself honestly.

task.title: Map your starting network
task.brief: List the people you already know and choose three to contact with a giving-first message.
steps: Write a list of 15 people: teachers, seniors, classmates, relatives' colleagues, internship contacts.
Mark five as weak ties working in or near your target field.
Write a one-line networking goal for three months.
Choose three people and write one useful thing you could share or ask for each.
checklist: My goal is specific and dated
I planned a giving-first step for three people
task.evidencePrompt: Write your goal and the three people with the step for each.

options: Looking for ways to be useful before asking for help
quiz.why: You contribute and build goodwill first, so later requests feel natural.

quiz.prompt: Why do weak ties often help find opportunities?
options: They move in different circles with different information
quiz.why: Weak ties reach circles you do not, so they hear about things you would miss.

quiz.prompt: A good networking goal is specific and has a time limit; for example, "meet four people in SAP in three ____". (one word)
quiz.why: A time frame makes the goal measurable and prompts action.

quiz.prompt: Which is a good first place to look for contacts?
options: College alumni and teachers, where trust already exists
quiz.why: Shared institutions create trust, so alumni and teachers often respond.

bank.prompt: You want to learn about careers in data analytics but know nobody. What is a sensible starting step?
options: Ask your placement cell for alumni in analytics and join one community
Wait until you have a job
Post that you need a job
bank.why: Starting with institutional links and a community gives warm, relevant entry points.

bank.prompt: Sharing a helpful article with a thank-you note is an example of ____ first. (one word)
bank.why: Giving first means offering value before asking for anything.

bank.prompt: Which networking message shows a clear goal?
options: I am exploring SAP ABAP roles and would value ten minutes about your first year
bank.why: It states why you are writing and what small thing you ask.

cards.back: Offering something useful, such as a resource, thanks or help, before asking for anything. It builds goodwill that makes later requests natural.

cards.front: What are weak ties and why do they matter?
cards.back: Acquaintances outside your close circle. They connect you to different groups and information, so they often bring job leads.

cards.front: What does a good networking goal look like?
cards.back: One specific, time-bound line, such as meeting four SAP professionals in three months to learn what the job involves.

cards.front: Where can a student find people?
cards.back: College teachers, seniors and alumni, student clubs and communities, online forums and professional networks, workshops and webinars.

reflection: Who among your acquaintances may know something useful about your target career, and what could you offer them first?

keyPoints: Networking means genuine relationships, not collecting favours.
Give first with small, real contributions.
Set a specific goal and start where trust already exists.
revision.redo: Name one weak tie and one useful thing you could share with them this week.
